name: Project A — Environment / World Study
prompt:
**The anchor (locked):** the **House of Wisdom, Baghdad, 8th to 13th century.** It is the great translation school and round library of the Islamic Golden Age, the place where the world's knowledge was gathered and translated. Warm, intellectual, clean, and something this cohort already half-knows from film and games. That's your world. I build the base scene, a couple of related environments, and a one-page style-and-palette guide, and you take **one sub-location** inside it.

**Pick one sub-location to own (or propose one that fits):**

- the **round library** — the circular reading hall, the heart of the place
- the **translation school** — a long working room, desks, scholars, a wall of texts
- the **bazaar** — a covered market that feeds the institution, mixed classes, full of life
- the **canalside** — the water edge, boats, light on a quay

**Sample story beats to hang your location on** (from the class prompt bank — the beat supplies the story, you supply the design):

- *the moment a scholar brings in a text no one here has seen, and the room tilts to look at it.*
- *a new arrival, first sight of the round library from the stair, the roof opening to the sky.*
- *the bazaar at the hour the scholars come to buy, ink and paper and argument all in one lane.*

> **Content note:** this anchor is clean-content. If your beat or sub-location edges toward a heavier historical layer (conflict, loss, conquest), **lead with the design question and the hook** — the space, the light, the story beat — and treat the sensitive context as optional background you may or may not draw on. The design carries the grade, not the history lesson.

**The one thing I want you to hear before you start:** your location is a *beat*, not a postcard. A beat has a before-and-after, a thing that just happened or is about to. "A library" is a noun. "The room the moment the rare text lands on the table" is a beat. That's the difference, and it's the whole project.

> **Aside (further reading):** *Dream Worlds: Production Design for Animation* by Hans Bacher, **Chapter 3, "Visual Development and Research."** That is exactly the stage you are in right now — translating a story idea into a look, before there's time left for studying. Good companion for picking your beat.
brief:
*The House of Wisdom, Baghdad. One shared world, one story beat each.*

Why this project, in one breath: this is the first time you are doing visual development the way a studio actually runs it. Not "I made a pretty scene" — "I made one believable location that fits a world the whole team is building, and I explored three to five real directions before I picked one." right? That's the job. And 3D is what lets you do it in a Friday instead of a fortnight. Get it?

## What you're making

You design **one location, as a story beat**, inside a shared reference world that I build once and hand to the class. You block it, you explore it from a few genuinely different directions, you pick the one that carries the beat, and you present the survivor with a hero render plus a paintover. You are not making a photoreal city. You are making a place that reads as a place, and a choice that reads as a choice.

## Guardrail menu

What's on the table, and the manual fallback if a tool is down. Every tool is **available**, never a hard dependency.

| Tool / technique | What it does for this project | Manual fallback (if it's down) |
|---|---|---|
| **Starter Scene** | One click: organized collections, a camera plus a three-point light rig, sane EEVEE/render settings, naming conventions. | Start from a fresh file; create a `00_world`, `10_set`, `20_light`, `30_cam` collection set by hand; add a camera and a key/fill/rim from the lamp menu. |
| **Quick Sheet renderer** | A contact sheet of 3 to 5 directional studies in one render (multiple angles or multiple lights, low samples). | Set up 3 to 5 cameras around the blockout, render each to its own PNG, and lay them in a grid in your 2D app. Same sheet, more steps. |
| **File / scene auditor** | Checks naming, orphan data, collection hygiene before delivery. | Manually rename everything, delete orphan materials/objects (clear stray parents with `Alt+P`, then purge from the outliner), and confirm each collection has a purpose. |
| **Palette extractor** (optional) | Pulls swatches from a render for the mood board. | Eyeball your hero render and pick 3 to 5 hex values by hand in your 2D app. |
| **Add-on allow-list** | Smart UV Project, BlenderKit (props, HDRI, materials), a studio light kit, optionally Node Tools. Pinned, offline-bundled. | Model the few hero props yourself; use a sky texture or a solid HDRI from the Extensions platform; three-point rig from lamps. |
| **Paintover (required)** | Your design pass over the 3D render, in your preferred 2D app. | Any 2D app you own: **Photoshop, Procreate, Clip Studio** — the skill is the paintover, not the app. |
| **Render** | **EEVEE** for daily iteration; Cycles-class only for the one hero pass. | If EEVEE feels soft, bump samples and turn on GI; the hero pass can be a longer Cycles-class render. |

Use it for the reasoning (why a light reads this way), not as a click-by-click map.

## Deliverables

- One **blocked location** with legible scale and flow, that fits the shared world's style.
- **3 to 5 directional studies** (light / composition / palette) — a genuine range, not five near-identical renders.
- **1 hero render + a paintover.** The paintover is required and emphasized; it shows design intent beyond the render.
- A **mood / art-direction board** — palette, references, 3 to 5 swatches.
- A clean **.blend**, auditor-checked (naming, collections, no orphan data).

Not required: photoreal, full detail, 4K. This is a study, and studies are allowed to be honest.

## Checkpoints

Two in-class checkpoints. Each gates on a **working artifact**, not on the clock. Before you show me, answer the self-checks — out loud to yourself is fine, the point is that you can.

### A1 — Blockout review (Wk 2)

- **What to show:** the blocked location — a rough 3D version that already has a sense of scale and a path the eye can walk.
- **Pass question:** does this read as a *place with a beat*, or as a *thing in a room*?
- **Self-check before you show me:**
  1. Where is the focal point, and what pulls the eye there — the light, a line, a size jump? Name one.
  2. What is the one thing you would **cut** to make the beat land harder?
  3. If I dropped a human in for scale, does the space feel right, too big, or too small? What gives it away?

### A2 — Directional-study review (Wk 3)

- **What to show:** your 3 to 5 directional studies on the Quick Sheet.
- **Pass question:** do these read as **different directions**, or as the same render five times with the light nudged?
- **Self-check before you show me:**
  1. Point at the one that's most different from the others. What is it actually changing — light, or camera, or palette?
  2. Which one would you **kill**, and why is it the weakest?
  3. If I couldn't see the labels, could I tell that each is a different *choice* rather than a different *time of day*?

### Delivery — Wk 4

Hero render plus paintover, the mood board, and the clean .blend. A short talk-through, and here's the honest bit: I want to hear the *process*, not the polish. What you killed and why is more interesting to me than the finished image.

> **Aside (further reading):** *3D Environment Design with Blender* by Abdelilah Hamdani — the layout, scale, and composition chapters fit this project directly. It's written for a recent Blender, so closer to 5.x than the EEVEE book above; still, expect the menu layout to have shifted a little.

> **Aside (further reading):** *How to Render: The Fundamentals of Light and Shadow and Reflectivity* by Scott Robertson and Thomas Bertling, **Chapter 2, "Light Types and Casting Shadows."** The hard/soft, rim, and occlusion vocabulary there is the same vocabulary your light rig is speaking. Worth a pass before A1.

## Assessment focus

For this project the four rubric dimensions land like this:

- **Design range:** the studies are a genuine spread of light/composition/palette, not five copies of one good idea.
- **Decision quality:** you can say why this beat, why this direction won, and what you cut and why.
- **Execution + presentation:** the blockout has legible scale and flow, the hero render reads, the paintover shows intent, and the .blend is clean enough to hand to someone else.
- **Iteration evidence:** A1 to A2 to delivery is a visible climb — each stage built on the last, with the weak directions shown as *killed*, not hidden.

Many good studies beat one perfect render. That is not a slogan. That is the grade.

## Revisit (spacing hook)

Remember that scale problem from your first blockout, the one where everything was the wrong length? It's back, wearing a different hat — now it's deciding whether your round library reads as *grand* or as *a hallway*. Same muscle. Point the eye, then size the space. We'll meet it again in Project C, where it decides whether a camera feels motivated or just parked.

*Next: Project B — where the location gets a character or a prop to live in it. The djinn is the lead, but you pick what to design. More on that in brief B.*

---

**Three lines to close, specific to this week:**
- **What I did:** I picked my sub-location and my beat, and I blocked it so the eye has somewhere to go.
- **What I learned:** a beat is a before-and-after, and the location is just the stage it happens on.
- **What I'd try next:** a different light direction, or one thing cut, to see if the beat lands harder than I think it does.

*No question is a dumb one here. If a panel moved and you can't find it, that's a 5.x thing, not a you thing. Ask.*
rubric:
*The House of Wisdom, Baghdad. Fall 2026. This is the rubric for Project A, applied to the environment study, the two checkpoints, and the delivery. Read it like a conversation, not a form.*

This rubric is Project A's cut of the term-wide one. The four dimensions are the same, but here they land on a *location as a story beat*, not an abstract idea. You'll use it to **self-assess before I ever see your work**, and then I'll give my view on top. That order is not a formality. Judging your own work first is what turns a student into someone who can take a brief and run with it. The term-wide version, with the dimension definitions and the 60/40 logic in full, lives next to this one in [rubric.md](./rubric.md). This one is the same four questions, aimed at your room. right?

## What you're delivering (checklist)

Hold yourself to this list before delivery. If a line is missing, that's a finding, and it's the best possible time to find it, because it's a checklist and not a grade.

- **One blocked location** with legible scale and flow, that fits the shared world's style. A beat, not a postcard.
- **3 to 5 directional studies** on a contact sheet, a genuine range of light, composition, and palette. Different decisions, not five near-identical renders.
- **One hero render plus a paintover.** The paintover is required. It shows the design intent that the render can't say on its own.
- **A mood / art-direction board**, the palette, the references, and three to five swatches. The argument for the look.
- **A clean .blend**, auditor-checked. Named, organized, no orphan data, so someone else could open it and not cry.
- **A talk-through at delivery.** The process, not the polish. What you killed and why is the half that carries you.

## The four dimensions, applied to A

The weights are the term-wide weights. The *what I'm looking for* is what they mean on an environment. Keep the 20 / 20 / 30 / 30 split in your head, because it's the shape of the grade, and it's where the 60/40 tilt shows.

### Design range (20%)

**What I'm looking for:** three to five directional studies that are actually *different*, different light, different camera, different palette. The range shows you were thinking in options, not defending one. It's not the count, it's the variety. A study of one, done five times, is not a range.

- **Strong:** I can tell each study is a *choice*, not a time of day. Warm, wide, grounded, and cool, tight, tense, and golden-hour, story-driven. Each one moves light, material, and palette together, because they're one mood. That's range.
- **Not there yet:** five renders of the same good idea, with the light nudged. The work looks nice and says one thing. You made a picture, not a set of options, and the choice between them was never really a choice.

### Decision quality (20%)

**What I'm looking for:** a reason you can state for every choice that matters. Why this beat, why this direction won, what you cut and why, why the focal point is there, why the palette does that. Kill/keep reasoning is visible, and the intent is legible to a stranger.

- **Strong:** the one-sentence *what it's about* is real, and the light, the material, and the palette all serve it. The paintover fixes the two or three spots that were holding back, and you can say *why* each fix. When I ask *why this one and not the other two*, the answer is a reason, not a feeling.
- **Not there yet:** choices that read as accidents, or as "it looked good." The room is fine but you can't defend it. The beat is there but you can't say *what it's about*, and a location without a beat is a room, not a story. That's the gap, and it's a fixable one.

### Execution + presentation (30%)

**What I'm looking for:** it reads. The blockout has scale and a path the eye can walk. The hero render reads small. The paintover shows intent. The board says why the look. The .blend is clean enough to hand to someone else. The craft of *showing* the work is half this dimension, and it's not decoration, it's communication.

- **Strong:** the blockout holds a human and points somewhere. The hero has a 1-2-3 read, bright, mid, dark, that the eye takes in at a glance. The paintover fixed a value, a focal point, and a palette, in that order. The board has the swatches, a reference or two, and the one line. The file is named and organized, and the weak directions are in there, shown as *killed*, not hidden.
- **Not there yet:** the idea is there but the presentation buries it. A great beat trapped behind an unlabeled sheet. A good design lost in a file with forty materials named `Material.047`. The render is pretty but the paintover is twenty random strokes, which is noise on top of a picture, not a decision.

### Iteration evidence (30%)

**What I'm looking for:** the climb, visible. A1 blockout, then A2 directional studies, then the hero, each stage built on the last. The weak directions are shown as *killed*, not hidden. The Quick Sheets and the failed takes are there, and they tell a story: you tried, you checked, you cut, you committed.

- **Strong:** I can see you kill the nudge and keep the real alternative. The paintover list shows you knew *what to fix and why* before you touched a brush. The board is the argument you built over three weeks, not a garnish you added on Friday. That's the work, and it's the most valuable part of the term.
- **Not there yet:** only the survivor. The hero is there and the process isn't, which means I can't see how you got there, and I can't tell a good decision from a lucky one. A beautiful render with an invisible climb is the one I have to ask questions about, and the questions are the part you should have been able to answer yourself.

## The two checkpoint gates

Both gate on a **working artifact, not on time**. You can't coast, and you can't be punished for a week being slow. Hit the pass question, move on. Miss it, we fix it in class, and that fix is part of your iteration evidence, not a penalty. Answer the self-checks before you show me, out loud to yourself is fine. The point is that you can.

### A1 — Blockout review (Wk 2, Sept 18)

- **What to show:** the blocked location, a rough 3D version that already has a sense of scale and a path the eye can walk.
- **Pass question:** does this read as a *place with a beat*, or as a *thing in a room*?
- **Self-check before you show me:**
  1. Where is the focal point, and what pulls the eye there, the light, a line, a size jump? Name one.
  2. What is the one thing you would **cut** to make the beat land harder?
  3. If I dropped a human in for scale, does the space feel right, too big, or too small? What gives it away?

### A2 — Directional-study review (Wk 3, Sept 25)

- **What to show:** your 3 to 5 directional studies on the contact sheet.
- **Pass question:** do these read as **different directions**, or as the same render five times with the light nudged?
- **Self-check before you show me:**
  1. Point at the one that's most different from the others. What is it actually changing, light, or camera, or palette?
  2. Which one would you **kill**, and why is it the weakest?
  3. If I couldn't see the labels, could I tell that each is a different *choice* rather than a different *time of day*?

### Delivery A (Wk 4, Oct 2)

The hero render plus the paintover, the mood board, the clean .blend, and the talk-through. Bring the A2 file, because the hero is built on the winner, the paintover is built on the hero, and the board is built on both. One file, three weeks, three layers of thinking. At delivery, I want the *process*, not the polish. What you killed and why is more interesting than the finished image.

## The 60/40 tilt, where it lands on A

The program leans on **design thinking and iteration** over **technical execution and presentation**. In these four dimensions, that works out to Design range (20) plus Decision quality (20) plus Iteration evidence (30) equal to **70%**, the design-thinking side, weighted a little heavier because iteration is where the real learning shows. Execution + presentation (30) is the **technical side**. So the tilt holds, and it's visible in the weights.

Practically: a student with a rough render and a brilliant process, and a student with a brilliant render and no process, are not the same grade. **The process wins.** If your hero is soft but your reasoning is sharp, and you can say *why this beat, why this direction, what you cut and why*, you are closer to the grade than you think. That's the design, not an oversight. It's the reason the paintover and the board are deliverables, because they're where the thinking shows.

## Self-assess before I see it (Project A)

These are the Boud moves, the ones that make you the person doing the judging, not the one being judged. Answer them in your 3-line reflection, honestly, before you hand the work over. I read them, and I'll tell you where my view matches yours and where it doesn't. That comparison is worth more than either one alone. You don't need to be self-critical to be honest. These are not a trap. They're the same questions I'd ask at a desk.

- **What changed between your A1 blockout and your delivery, and why?** If the answer is "I made it prettier," that's execution. If it's "I cut the weak direction and the beat got clearer," that's design. I want to hear which one.
- **What's the one-sentence *what it's about* for your location, and does the render actually show it?** If the sentence says *a secret canalside* and the render says *a flat harbor*, the paintover should have closed that gap. Did it?
- **Which of your directional studies is the weakest, and what specifically is weak about it?** Naming your own weak work, precisely, is the whole of decision quality. You don't have to fix it. Just be able to say why it's the one you'd cut.
- **What would you change with another week?** A student who says "I'm done" has stopped looking. A student who names one specific next move, a fourth direction, a different light, one thing cut, is still thinking, and that's the one I want to see.

---

**One line to carry out of this rubric:** the grade is not the render. The grade is the thinking you can defend, the decisions you can explain, and the evidence that you got there by working, not by luck. Everything else in this document is just the shape of that, aimed at your room.

name: Project B — Character or Prop Design Package (Funpacks)
prompt:
**Pick one of three genre tracks, then pick your subject within it.** The subject is a starting point, not a mandate. You have full choice of *what* to design, even within a genre.

1. **Horror.** A creature, a cursed or haunted object, or a "the other" figure. **Design-level menace only** — shape, silhouette, and wrongness, not gore. If the idea needs a wound to work, it isn't the idea yet. Find the menace in the silhouette first.

2. **Comedy.** A gag prop, an exasperated sidekick, or an absurd machine or creature. It must **read in silhouette and expression** — if the joke only lands with a caption, the design isn't carrying it.

3. **Mythic / folklore.** A **non-western** figure or artifact that this western, Canadian cohort already knows through film, games, and anime. This is where the **House of Wisdom orbit** anchors you, so it can sit inside Project A's world. The **djinn / genie** is the lead, but you have full choice of what to design: the djinn *itself*, or something **around it** — its **vessel or lamp**, a **magical astrolabe** prop, a **guardian of the library**, a **scholar-summoner**, or a **simurgh**. Other strong anchors: a **kitsune or yokai** (Japanese), a **feathered-serpent or jaguar deity** (Mesoamerican), a **koi or dragon**, a **Polynesian demigod**.

> **Content note:** keep horror and comedy at the **design level** — shape, silhouette, menace, expression, absurdity — not graphic. Where the subject carries a historical or cultural weight, **lead with the design question and the hook**, and treat the deeper context as optional background you may or may not draw on. The design carries the grade. And because the subject can be a figure from a specific culture, do the small amount of research that keeps it from being a costume — a real simurgh is a griffin-with-a-human-head, not a generic dragon in a hat. That care is visible, and it's part of the craft.

**The one thing I want you to hear before you start:** a funpack is not a portrait. It is a *specification*. When a production artist looks at your sheet, they should be able to rebuild your subject in another shot, in another scene, from that sheet alone. If the back view is a mystery, the design isn't finished. right? That's the bar.

> **Aside (further reading):** *Framed Ink: Drawing and Composition for Visual Storytellers* by Marcos Mateu-Mestre, **Chapter 5, Character Design (silhouette and expression).** "Overall silhouette" and "dynamics of expression" are the two words this whole project is built on. Worth a read before you block anything.
brief:
*One subject, presented the way a studio would hand it off.*

Why this project, in one breath: last week you built a place. This week you build the thing that lives in it — a character or a prop — and you present it as a **funpack**, the turnaround-and-studies sheet a production actually uses. The difference from a pretty render is the sheet. A render shows one angle; a funpack says *this is the design, from every angle, and here is how it behaves.* Get it? That's the deliverable.

## What you're making

You design **one character or one prop**, develop it in 3D, and present it as a production-ready reference sheet: a 3-view turnaround, a set of expressions or variants, a silhouette check, and one or two material directions, capped with two hero renders. You are not making a game-ready model or a rig. You are making a design that reads, and a sheet that communicates it. That's the whole thing.

## The prompt

**Pick one of three genre tracks, then pick your subject within it.** The subject is a starting point, not a mandate. You have full choice of *what* to design, even within a genre.

1. **Horror.** A creature, a cursed or haunted object, or a "the other" figure. **Design-level menace only** — shape, silhouette, and wrongness, not gore. If the idea needs a wound to work, it isn't the idea yet. Find the menace in the silhouette first.

2. **Comedy.** A gag prop, an exasperated sidekick, or an absurd machine or creature. It must **read in silhouette and expression** — if the joke only lands with a caption, the design isn't carrying it.

3. **Mythic / folklore.** A **non-western** figure or artifact that this western, Canadian cohort already knows through film, games, and anime. This is where the **House of Wisdom orbit** anchors you, so it can sit inside Project A's world. The **djinn / genie** is the lead, but you have full choice of what to design: the djinn *itself*, or something **around it** — its **vessel or lamp**, a **magical astrolabe** prop, a **guardian of the library**, a **scholar-summoner**, or a **simurgh**. Other strong anchors: a **kitsune or yokai** (Japanese), a **feathered-serpent or jaguar deity** (Mesoamerican), a **koi or dragon**, a **Polynesian demigod**.

> **Content note:** keep horror and comedy at the **design level** — shape, silhouette, menace, expression, absurdity — not graphic. Where the subject carries a historical or cultural weight, **lead with the design question and the hook**, and treat the deeper context as optional background you may or may not draw on. The design carries the grade. And because the subject can be a figure from a specific culture, do the small amount of research that keeps it from being a costume — a real simurgh is a griffin-with-a-human-head, not a generic dragon in a hat. That care is visible, and it's part of the craft.

**The one thing I want you to hear before you start:** a funpack is not a portrait. It is a *specification*. When a production artist looks at your sheet, they should be able to rebuild your subject in another shot, in another scene, from that sheet alone. If the back view is a mystery, the design isn't finished. right? That's the bar.

> **Aside (further reading):** *Framed Ink: Drawing and Composition for Visual Storytellers* by Marcos Mateu-Mestre, **Chapter 5, Character Design (silhouette and expression).** "Overall silhouette" and "dynamics of expression" are the two words this whole project is built on. Worth a read before you block anything.

- **Not there yet:** five faces that are the same face with a different mouth, or one material with the roughness nudged. The work looks nice and says one thing. You made a portrait, not a set of options, and the choice between them was never really a choice.

### Decision quality (20%)

**What I'm looking for:** the genre's intent, menace, comedy, or myth, in the *design, not stuck on top of it*, and a reason you can state for every choice. The craft of *showing* the work is half this dimension, and a funpack that a production artist could rebuild from, alone, is the whole point.

- **Strong:** the turnaround is built from clean, readable volumes, not a soup. The silhouette check shows the subject reads in solid black, from front, side, and back. ## The four dimensions, applied to C

The weights are the term-wide weights. The *what I'm looking for* is what they mean on a scene. Keep the 20 / 20 / 30 / 30 split in your head, because it's the shape of the grade, and it's where the 60/40 tilt shows.

### Design range (20%)

**What I'm looking for:** a *sequence* of different framings and purposes, establishing, beat, reveal, each earning its place. Not the same wide shot three times. The range shows you were thinking in a *story*, not defending one framing.

- **Strong:** the shots are a sequence with a before and an after. The establishing sets the world, the beat does the moving, the reveal lands the moment. Each one is a different *choice* of framing and purpose, and cut any one and the story loses something. And the light / mood turn gives the sequence a before and an after in *feeling* too, a start mood and an end mood with a reason behind the change, not just a light that happened to shift. That's range.
- **Not there yet:** a pile of nice framings with no sequence. Three wides of the same moment, or a close-up that doesn't earn its place. The work looks nice and says one thing, one framing, and the order was never really a story. A shot list is not a confusion, and if yours reads as a confusion, the range is missing.

### Decision quality (20%)

**What I'm looking for:** every camera motivated, the 180-degree line respected, and the genre and tone from A and B reading clearly through the choices. Why this height, this distance, this angle, tied to the beat. The intent is legible to a stranger.

- **Strong:** I can name the motivation of every camera, what in the scene justifies it being exactly there. The line is respected, and if I had to cross it, I reset the geography first. The beat from A and the subject from B are doing the story, and the cameras are serving them, not the other way around. When I ask *why this shot and not the one before it*, the answer is a reason. And I can name the light / mood turn, what changes from beat to beat, why it's the right turn, and what I chose to hold so the audience has something to follow it against, a reasoned turn, not just *the light changed*.
- **Not there yet:** a camera parked in a pretty spot for no reason. A line crossed that flips the geography, and the audience loses the scene. A framing that's good because it looked good, and the order is an accident. The scene is there but you can't say *why the camera is where it is*, and a motivated camera is the whole grade of this project. That's the gap, and it's a fixable one.

### Execution + presentation (30%)

**What I'm looking for:** the contact sheet is labeled and in story order, the light / mood turn reads legibly on it, the paintover adds intent, and the .blend is clean. The label on each frame matters as much as the frame, because that's how a production reads it. The craft of *showing* the work is half this dimension, and it's communication, not decoration.

- **Strong:** the sheet reads left to right as a story, establishing, beat, reveal, each one labeled. The light / mood turn reads clearly on it, in order, a before and an after in feeling, so the sequence reads as one scene moving through a change, not several disconnected days. The paintover added the design accents that the blockout couldn't. The file is named and organized, and the cut shots are in there, shown as *killed*, not hidden.
- **Not there yet:** an unlabeled contact sheet, where I can't tell a beat from a reveal. A turn that isn't there, or that shifts without a reason, so the sequence reads as several disconnected days. The blockout is there but the paintover is missing, so the design intent is invisible. A great scene trapped behind an unreadable sheet.

### Iteration evidence (30%)

**What I'm looking for:** the climb, visible. C1 shot list, then C2 blockout and cameras, then the delivery, each stage built on the last. The shot list got cut and re-ordered, the weak cameras got removed, and the process is legible in what survived.

- **Strong:** I can see you cut the shot you'd lose nothing by removing, and re-order the rest until the story moved. The 180-degree line is there, and it changed a camera, and the weak framing is in there, shown as *killed*, not hidden. The talk-through tells the story of the cut, which is the most valuable part of the term.
- **Not there yet:** only the survivor. The contact sheet is there and the process isn't, which means I can't see how you got there, and I can't tell a motivated camera from a lucky one. A beautiful sequence with an invisible climb is the one I have to ask questions about, and the questions are the part you should have been able to answer yourself.

Both gate on a **working artifact, not on time**. You can't coast, and you can't be punished for a week being slow. Hit the pass question, move on. Miss it, we fix it in class, and that fix is part of your iteration evidence, not a penalty. Answer the self-checks before you show me. The point is that you can.

### C2 — Blockout + camera review (Wk 12, Nov 27)

- **Pass question:** is the camera **motivated and continuous**, or is it parked in pretty spots?

The bar is one line: a stranger watching your frames in order should understand the beat, the tone, why the camera is where it is, and what changes in the feeling across the scene and why. The turn must be articulable, not just present.

## The 60/40 tilt, where it lands on C

The program leans on **design thinking and iteration** over **technical execution and presentation**. In these four dimensions, that works out to Design range (20) plus Decision quality (20) plus Iteration evidence (30) equal to **70%**, the design-thinking side, weighted a little heavier because iteration is where the real learning shows. Execution + presentation (30) is the **technical side**. So the tilt holds, and it's visible in the weights.

Practically: a student with a rough blockout and a brilliant sequence, and a student with a polished blockout and no sequence, are not the same grade. **The process wins.** And the line that does the most work on C: **motivated is the whole grade of this project.** If your scene is rough but you can say *why each camera is where it is and why the line held and what you cut*, you are closer to the grade than you think. That's the design, not an oversight. It's the reason the contact sheet is labeled and the talk-through is a deliverable, because they're where the thinking shows.

## Self-assess before I see it (Project C)

These are the Boud moves, the ones that make you the person doing the judging, not the one being judged. Answer them in your 3-line reflection, honestly, before you hand the work over. I read them, and I'll tell you where my view matches yours and where it doesn't. That comparison is worth more than either one alone. You don't need to be self-critical to be honest. These are not a trap.

- **What changed between your C1 shot list and your delivery, and why?** If the answer is "I made it prettier," that's execution. If it's "I cut the weak shot and re-ordered the rest and the beat moved," that's design. I want to hear which one.
- **For each camera, what's the motivation, and does the 180-degree line hold across all of them?** If a camera is parked in a pretty spot for no reason, name it. If the line flipped the geography, name where. A motivated camera is the grade, and an unmotivated one is the gap.
- **Which of your shots is the weakest, and what specifically is weak about it?** Naming your own weak work, precisely, is the whole of decision quality. You don't have to fix it. Just be able to say why it's the one you'd cut.
- **What is the light / mood turn, and can you defend it?** Name it out loud: what changes from beat to beat, how it changes, why it's the right turn, and what you held so the scene still reads as one. If you can only say *the light changed* and not why, the turn is a guess, and a guess you can name is a decision you can make.
- **What would you change with another week?** A student who says "I'm done" has stopped looking. A student who names one specific next move, a fourth shot, a different lens, a re-order, is still thinking, and that's the one I want to see.

---

**One line to carry out of this rubric:** the grade is not the render. The grade is the thinking you can defend, the decisions you can explain, and the evidence that you got there by working, not by luck. And on C, the one line that does the most work: motivated is the whole grade. A stranger watching your frames in order should understand the beat, the tone, and why the camera is where it is. Everything else in this document is just the shape of that, aimed at your scene.
